question: In the lecture we saw that if a function \(f\) has a relative maximum at a point \(c\) inside an open interval \((a,b)\) and is differentiable at \(c\), then \(f'(c)=0\). Using the limit definition of the derivative from the definition context, explain why the left‑hand and right‑hand limits of the difference quotient must both be zero.
answer: Because for \(x<c\) we have \(f(x)\le f(c)\), the numerator \(f(x)-f(c)\le0\) while the denominator \(x-c<0\), so the quotient is \(\ge0\). As \(x\to c^-\) the quotient is bounded below by \(0\) and above by \(0\), forcing the left‑hand limit to be \(0\). Similarly, for \(x>c\) the numerator is \(\le0\) and the denominator \(>0\), so the quotient is \(\le0\); the right‑hand limit is also forced to be \(0\). Hence the two one‑sided limits coincide at \(0\), giving \(f'(c)=0\).

question: The lecture states that for a relative maximum at \(c\) inside an open interval \((a,b)\) we can choose \(\delta>0\) such that \((c-\delta,c+\delta)\subset(a,b)\). Explain why the openness of \((a,b)\) guarantees the existence of such a \(\delta\), referencing the definition of an open set in the context of intervals.
answer: An open set is defined by the property that every point in it has a neighborhood entirely contained in the set. Since \(c\in(a,b)\) and \((a,b)\) is open, there exists \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \((c-\varepsilon,c+\varepsilon)\subset(a,b)\). Taking \(\delta=\varepsilon\) (or the minimum of this \(\varepsilon\) and any other required \(\delta\)) provides the desired interval \((c-\delta,c+\delta)\) lying inside \((a,b)\).

In the product rule derivation, the difference quotient for \(f\cdot g\) splits into two terms: \(\displaystyle \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c}g(x)\) and \(f(c)\frac{g(x)-g(c)}{x-c}\).  As \(x\to c\), the first factor tends to \(f'(c)\) and \(g(x)\) tends to \(g(c)\) by continuity, while the second factor tends to \(g'(c)\).  Thus the whole expression tends to \(f'(c)g(c)+f(c)g'(c)\), proving that \((f\cdot g)'(c)\) exists.

answer: Rolle’s theorem requires a function to be continuous on a closed interval \([a,b]\) and differentiable on the open interval \((a,b)\).  The function \(f(x)=1-|x|\) is continuous on \([-1,1]\) but fails to be differentiable at the endpoints \(-1\) and \(1\) because the left and right derivatives at those points do not exist.  Since the differentiability condition is violated, the theorem cannot be applied, and consequently there is no guarantee of a point \(c\in(-1,1)\) where \(f'(c)=0\).  This explains why the conclusion of Rolle’s theorem fails for this continuous function.

question: If \(f\) is increasing on \([a,b]\) and differentiable, can we conclude that \(f' \ge 0\) everywhere? Use the mean value theorem to justify your answer.
answer: Yes. For any \(x<y\), the mean value theorem gives a \(c\) with \(f(y)-f(x)=f'(c)(y-x)\). Since \(f\) is increasing, \(f(y)-f(x)\ge 0\), and \(y-x>0\), so \(f'(c)\ge 0\). As this holds for all pairs \(x<y\), \(f'\ge 0\) everywhere.

question: Suppose \(f\) is constant on the open interval \((a,b)\) and satisfies \(f(a)=f(b)=0\). Using the fact that the derivative of a constant function is zero, argue why \(f\) must be identically zero on \((a,b)\). Then discuss whether the same conclusion would hold if \(f\) were only defined on \((a,b)\) without the endpoint values, and why the open interval condition is essential.
answer: If \(f\) is constant on \((a,b)\), then by definition \(f(x)=k\) for all \(x\in(a,b)\). The derivative of a constant function is zero everywhere, so \(f'(x)=0\) for all \(x\in(a,b)\). Since \(f(a)=f(b)=0\) and the function is constant on the open interval, the constant must be zero, giving \(f(x)=0\) for all \(x\in(a,b)\). If the function were only defined on \((a,b)\) without endpoint values, we could not conclude that the constant equals zero; the function could be any constant. The open interval condition is essential because it allows us to use the derivative definition (which requires points on both sides of \(c\)) and to apply the continuity argument that forces the constant to match the endpoint values when they are known.

answer: For each \(n\), apply the mean value theorem to the interval \([x_n,c]\). There exists \(\xi_n\in(x_n,c)\) such that \(\displaystyle f'(\xi_n)=\frac{f(c)-f(x_n)}{c-x_n}\). As \(x_n\to c\), the points \(\xi_n\) also converge to \(c\). Since \(f\) is differentiable, \(f'(\xi_n)\to f'(c)\). Because \(f\) is increasing, \(f(c)-f(x_n)\ge0\) and \(c-x_n>0\), so each quotient is \(\ge0\). Hence the limit \(f'(c)\) is non‑negative.
